title: From Al-Imran to At-Tawbah
intro: 40 days through surahs 3 to 9, from Al-Imran to At-Tawbah, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: This plan walks through surahs 3 to 9, beginning with Al-Imran, "The Family of Imran": 200 verses revealed in Medina. Imran is understood as the father of Maryam (Mary), whose story the surah tells. This prayer belongs to people firm in knowledge, asking to keep the guidance they have been given. "The Bestower" is al-Wahhab.

The guardian of Maryam (Mary), the Prophet Zakariya (Zechariah), keeps finding food with her in the sanctuary, and she tells him it comes from Allah. Seeing this, the elderly prophet prays for a child of his own, though his wife is barren. The angels answer with news of a son, the Prophet Yahya (John).

Maryam (Mary) is the only woman the Quran mentions by name, and the 19th surah is named after her. Here the angels tell her she has been chosen, purified and honoured above the women of creation. The verses that follow announce the birth of her son, the Prophet Isa (Jesus).

Al-birr, translated here as "piety", means righteousness and goodness in the fullest sense. The verse ties it to giving away what one truly loves, not only what is left over. According to a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the companion Abu Talha responded by giving away his most prized orchard.

posts.display: And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate. And remember Allah's favour unto you: How ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts so that ye became as brothers by His grace.
posts.display_original: وَٱعْتَصِمُوا۟ بِحَبْلِ ٱللَّهِ جَمِيعًا وَلَا تَفَرَّقُوا۟ وَٱذْكُرُوا۟ نِعْمَتَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذْ كُنتُمْ أَعْدَآءً فَأَلَّفَ بَيْنَ قُلُوبِكُمْ فَأَصْبَحْتُم بِنِعْمَتِهِۦٓ إِخْوَٰنًا
posts.caption: "The cable of Allah" is habl Allah, a rope; commentators have explained it in several ways, including the Quran and Allah's covenant. The enemies who became brothers are linked by commentators with Aws and Khazraj, the two main Arab tribes of Medina, whose long feud ended when they embraced Islam.

posts.display: Those who spend (of that which Allah hath given them) in ease and in adversity, those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind; Allah loveth the good.
posts.caption: The verse before describes a paradise as wide as the heavens and the earth. This one describes who it is prepared for: people who give in good times and bad, hold back their anger, and forgive. "The good" renders al-muhsinin, those who practise ihsan, excellence in doing good.

Near the end of Al-Imran, these verses describe people who reflect on the sky and the earth and turn that reflection into prayer. According to a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once rose at night, looked up at the sky and recited this closing passage of the surah.

posts.display: O mankind! Be careful of your duty to your Lord Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate and from them twain hath spread abroad a multitude of men and women.
posts.display_original: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱتَّقُوا۟ رَبَّكُمُ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكُم مِّن نَّفْسٍ وَٰحِدَةٍ وَخَلَقَ مِنْهَا زَوْجَهَا وَبَثَّ مِنْهُمَا رِجَالًا كَثِيرًا وَنِسَآءً
posts.caption: An-Nisa, "The Women", is the fourth surah: 176 verses revealed in Medina, much of it on family, orphans and the rights of women. It opens by reminding all people of one shared origin, a single soul. Pickthall's "be careful of your duty" renders ittaqu, from taqwa, mindful awareness of Allah.

This verse closes a section of family law with a gentle note: the rules are meant to lighten burdens, because people were created weak. Commentators have understood that weakness in various ways, from frailty in the face of desire to human limits in general.

Amanat, "deposits" or trusts, covers anything placed in someone's care: property, responsibility, a secret. The verse joins honesty with trusts to justice in judgment. According to commentators such as Ibn Kathir, it was revealed when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ returned the keys of the Kaaba to their keeper, Uthman ibn Talha.

A verse about something everyday: the greeting. Muslims greet one another with as-salamu alaykum, "peace be upon you", and the verse calls for a reply at least as good, or better, such as adding "and the mercy of Allah". "Taketh count" means Allah keeps account of all things.

According to classical commentators, the passage around this verse concerns a theft in Medina and an attempt to pin it on an innocent man. Amid that, this verse holds the door open to anyone who has done wrong. Seeking forgiveness, istighfar, is a constant theme of the Quran.

A striking question: what would Allah gain by punishing anyone who is grateful and believes? "Responsive" renders Shakir, literally "the Thankful" or "the Appreciative", One who recognises and rewards even small good. It comes right after a passage on hypocrisy that ends with the door to repentance left open.

posts.display: But help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty. Help not one another unto sin and transgression.
posts.display_original: وَتَعَاوَنُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلْبِرِّ وَٱلتَّقْوَىٰ وَلَا تَعَاوَنُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلْإِثْمِ وَٱلْعُدْوَٰنِ
posts.caption: Al-Ma'idah, "The Table Spread", is the fifth surah: 120 verses from the Medinan period, and many scholars count it among the last surahs revealed. This line on cooperation comes in a verse about the pilgrimage, right after a warning not to let hatred of others push anyone into wrongdoing. "Pious duty" renders taqwa.

The Quran tells the story of the two sons of Adam, known in tradition as Qabil and Habil (Cain and Abel). When one brother's offering is accepted, the other threatens to kill him. These are the words of the brother who refuses to raise his hand, even under threat.

posts.display: Whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.
posts.display_original: مَن قَتَلَ نَفْسًۢا بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ أَوْ فَسَادٍ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًا وَمَنْ أَحْيَاهَا فَكَأَنَّمَآ أَحْيَا ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًا
posts.caption: This follows the story of the two sons of Adam. The verse says this was decreed for the Children of Israel, and a very similar teaching appears in the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law. It is one of the most quoted verses of the Quran on the sanctity of human life.

The surah's name comes from this story. The disciples of the Prophet Isa (Jesus) ask whether his Lord can send down a table spread with food from heaven, and he tells them to be mindful of Allah. In the verses that follow, Isa prays for the table as a feast and a sign, and Allah promises to send it down.

This verse belongs to the surah's closing scene, set on the Day of Judgment, where the truthful are rewarded. Its image of contentment flowing both ways, Allah pleased with them and they with Him, returns in several other surahs. One more verse, on Allah's sovereignty, ends the surah.

posts.display_original: ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَجَعَلَ ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ وَٱلنُّورَ ثُمَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ بِرَبِّهِمْ يَعْدِلُونَ
posts.caption: Al-An'am, "The Cattle", is a Meccan surah of 165 verses, named for the pagan customs about livestock it discusses. Some early reports say it was revealed all at once. It is one of five surahs that open with "Praise be to Allah", al-hamdu lillah; the others are Al-Fatiha, Al-Kahf, Saba and Fatir.

A lesser-known verse with a striking idea: every creature on land and every bird belongs to a community, umam, "peoples like unto you". Commentators explain that they too are created, provided for and known to Allah. "The Book" here refers to the record of His decrees.

posts.display: Not a leaf falleth but He knoweth it, not a grain amid the darkness of the earth, naught of wet or dry but (it is noted) in a clear record.
posts.display_original: وَمَا تَسْقُطُ مِن وَرَقَةٍ إِلَّا يَعْلَمُهَا وَلَا حَبَّةٍ فِى ظُلُمَٰتِ ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا رَطْبٍ وَلَا يَابِسٍ إِلَّا فِى كِتَٰبٍ مُّبِينٍ
posts.caption: The verse begins: "And with Him are the keys of the Invisible. None but He knoweth them." Then it moves from the vast to the tiny: land and sea, a falling leaf, a single grain in the dark soil. "A clear record" is understood as the record of all things kept with Allah.

The Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) looks at a star, then the moon, then the sun, and rejects each as a lord because each one sets. Commentators differ on whether he was reasoning his own way to faith or leading his people to see the flaw in worshipping the heavens. Three verses later he turns to the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

posts.display: Revile not those unto whom they pray beside Allah lest they wrongfully revile Allah through ignorance.
posts.display_original: وَلَا تَسُبُّوا۟ ٱلَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ فَيَسُبُّوا۟ ٱللَّهَ عَدْوًۢا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ
posts.caption: The first sentence of this verse forbids insulting what others worship, lest they insult Allah in return out of ignorance. Scholars have drawn from it a wider principle: avoiding words that lead to greater harm. It was revealed in Mecca, when the Muslims were a small and persecuted community.

A generous arithmetic: a good deed brings a tenfold reward, while a bad deed counts only as one. A well-known hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari adds that a good deed merely intended is recorded too, and that rewards can be multiplied far beyond ten. The verse ends with a promise of fairness.

Near the close of Al-An'am, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told to declare that his whole life belongs to Allah: prayer, sacrifice, living and dying. Many Muslims recite this verse in the supplication that opens their prayer. "Sacrifice" renders nusuk, which can also mean acts of devotion in general.

Al-A'raf, "The Heights", is a Meccan surah of 206 verses. It retells the story of the Prophet Adam and his wife, and this is their prayer after eating from the forbidden tree. Both admit the wrong together and ask for forgiveness and mercy. Many Muslims know this short prayer by heart.

"O Children of Adam" is a call to all humanity. Clothing is presented as a gift that covers and adorns, and then the verse points beyond it: the best garment is libas at-taqwa, "the raiment of restraint from evil", meaning mindfulness of Allah. "Splendid vesture" means fine clothing.

Al-A'raf takes its name from "the Heights", a place between the Garden and the Fire described a few verses earlier. Here it turns to prayer: call on Allah humbly and quietly. Many commentators, Ibn Kathir among them, read "aggressors" here as those who overstep proper limits, including in how they pray.

The Prophet Musa (Moses) returns from his meeting with Allah to find his people worshipping a calf. In his anger he seizes his brother, the Prophet Harun (Aaron), who explains that the people overpowered him. Musa's anger turns to prayer for them both. "Most Merciful of all who show mercy" is arham ar-rahimin.

"The fairest names" are al-asma al-husna, the Most Beautiful Names of Allah, such as the Merciful, the Forgiving and the Wise. A well-known hadith speaks of ninety-nine of them. Calling on Allah by His names is a central part of Muslim prayer and remembrance.

Near its end, Al-A'raf contrasts idols, which cannot even help themselves, with Allah. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told to declare where his own protection lies, and these are the words given to him. "Protecting Friend" renders wali, a guardian and close ally, and al-Wali is one of the names of Allah.

Three short instructions to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in one verse: hold to forgiveness, encourage what is good, and turn away from the ignorant. "Kindness" here renders al-urf, what is commonly recognised as good. Some classical scholars called it the most comprehensive verse in the Quran on good character.

posts.display: They only are the (true) believers whose hearts feel fear when Allah is mentioned, and when His revelations are recited unto them they increase their faith, and who trust in their Lord.
posts.caption: Al-Anfal, "The Spoils of War", is a Medinan surah of 75 verses, revealed after the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. Early on comes this portrait of believers: hearts that tremble at the mention of Allah, faith that grows on hearing His verses, and trust in Him, tawakkul.

In a run of verses addressed to the believers, Al-Anfal names the things people hold dearest, wealth and children, and calls them a fitnah: a test or trial. Commentators explain that the test lies in how these blessings are handled. Almost the same words appear in At-Taghabun 64:15, which likewise points to the "immense reward" with Allah.

A principle the Quran states twice, here and in Ar-Ra'd 13:11: Allah does not change the blessing He has given a people until they change what is within themselves. In context it explains the fall of earlier nations, such as Pharaoh's people, who rejected the signs they were given.

At-Tawbah, "Repentance", has 129 verses from late in the Medinan period. It is the only surah that does not open with the Bismillah, and scholars have given various reasons. This verse answers those who were glad when misfortune struck the believers: nothing happens except what Allah has decreed.

The surah's name comes from tawbah, turning back to Allah in repentance. This verse describes Allah as at-Tawwab, "the Relenting", the One who accepts repentance again and again. Commentators connect the passage with believers who had stayed behind from an expedition and then admitted their faults.

This follows the story of three companions who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk without excuse. One of them, Ka'b ibn Malik, chose to tell the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ the plain truth rather than invent excuses, and after fifty days their repentance was accepted. This verse comes right after it.

Near the end of At-Tawbah comes this portrait of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: one of the people themselves, grieved by their hardship, deeply concerned for them. "Full of pity, merciful" renders ra'uf and rahim, two words the Quran also uses of Allah.

The final verse of At-Tawbah: if people turn away, Allah is enough. Many Muslims repeat its words as part of their daily remembrance. That completes this journey through seven surahs, from Al-Imran to At-Tawbah. Thank you for reading along.
